title: Why Lomonosov plated ships with copper
topic: Why the 18th‑century Russian engineer Mikhail Lomonosov added copper plating to ship hulls (St. Petersburg, 1760s) to prevent bio‑fouling and increase speed

lines: A Russian engineer hammers copper plates onto a ship’s hull, sparks flying.
He aims to stop the invisible enemies that cling beneath the waves.
Fellow shipwrights laugh, warning the metal will rust and sink their fleet.
They claim the extra weight will slow every vessel to a crawl.
Lomonosov orders the copper nailed beneath the waterline in St. Petersburg.
The ship leaves the dock still covered in thick, green slime.
Barnacles and shipworm have already turned the hull into a barn.
You see how a greasy pan sticks to food – the slime drags a ship the same way.
Copper reacts with seawater, forming a thin copper‑oxy‑chloride film that is poisonous to marine life.
The film dissolves constantly, so barnacles and shipworm cannot attach.
With the slime gone, the hull slices through water, gaining precious speed.
The navy dubs the vessel ‘copper‑bottomed,’ a mark of quality that cuts insurance premiums.
Ironically, the same copper that saved speed later sparked a bolt‑corrosion crisis, forcing engineers to redesign fasteners.

claims.claim: Copper sheathing creates a poisonous copper‑oxy‑chloride film that deters shipworm and barnacles, reducing drag and increasing speed.
